title: At my table (2 Samuel 9)
hook: David seeks Jonathan's lame son and seats him at his table always

segments.voice: Yesterday David danced before the ark in a linen ephod. Your line was holding nothing back. Today, the king remembers an old promise.

A question, asked in a palace: is there anyone still left of the house of Saul, so I can show him kindness for Jonathan's sake? David is settled now, with a city and an army. A new king asking after the old king's family could sound like a threat. But David is remembering a field, and arrows, and an oath Jonathan made him swear: the Lord between me and you, between my children and your children. Someone remembers a name, a servant of Saul's house called Ziba. They send for him.
screen: `IS ANYONE LEFT OF SAUL'S HOUSE?` → `FOR JONATHAN'S SAKE.` → `SEND FOR ZIBA.`

segments.voice: Ziba says yes. There's a son of Jonathan, lame in his feet, living in someone else's house in a place called Lo-debar. His name is Mephibosheth. Earlier the book told how it happened: he was a small child when news came of the battle where his father and grandfather died, and his nurse snatched him up and ran, and he fell. David sends for him. Mephibosheth comes in and falls on his face, with every reason to be afraid. David says his name. Here is your servant, he answers. Then David tells him: fear not. I will surely show you kindness for Jonathan your father's sake. I'll give you back all the land of Saul, and you will eat bread at my table continually. The Hebrew for kindness here is chesed, loyal love, the faithfulness you owe because of a bond. When David first asked Ziba, he even called it the kindness of God. Mephibosheth can hardly take it in; he calls himself a dead dog. David doesn't argue. He just keeps the promise. Ziba's household will work the land, and Mephibosheth will eat at the king's table like one of the king's sons. The chapter ends with two facts side by side: he ate always at the king's table, and he was lame in both his feet. Nothing about him had to change to get a seat. The table changed. David kept faith with a friend who was gone by keeping a place for his son.
screen: `A SON OF JONATHAN, LAME IN HIS FEET.` · `FEAR NOT.` · `CHESED: LOYAL LOVE.` · then, large: `ALWAYS AT MY TABLE.` · then: `LIKE ONE OF THE KING'S SONS.`

segments.voice: Let one friend come to mind who has died, moved far away, or drifted out of touch, and think of the people they left behind: a partner, a child, a parent. Ask what a seat at your table would look like for one of them: a dinner, a message on the anniversary, a story about their person they haven't heard. If you pray, you can hold their names.
chesed. The loyal love David showed Jonathan's son Mephibosheth, giving him land back and a permanent seat at the king's table. Today's word.
Your line: always at my table. A promise kept for someone who's gone. Day seven hundred forty-five, done.

howItsDone: Jews read the story of Mephibosheth in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets, as an example of chesed, loyal kindness, kept across generations.

Mephibosheth asked for a seat first, and David couldn't refuse.
Mephibosheth had been healed, so he could now serve at court.

notes: Whole chapter paraphrased; no quotation marks used.
A general historical claim about kings removing rivals' heirs was cut under the claims rule.
Chesed glossed as loyal love; 'the kindness of God' is 9:3. Confirm.
Mephibosheth's fall is from 2 Samuel 4:4; his age there is left out.
Ziba's later conduct (2 Samuel 16, 19) is left out.
Editor: corrected attribution — in 9:3 it is David, not Ziba, who speaks of 'the kindness of God'; cut the unsourced 'Saul's family has scattered' from the hook.

Audit: the teach and a myth item (marked true) said David's first words to Mephibosheth were 'fear not'; in 9:6–7 David first says his name, Mephibosheth answers 'Behold thy servant', and only then 'Fear not'. Teach and myth corrected.
